transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-08-14
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~62 min
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Olivia Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (EchoWorks - ML Platform), Aaron Li (EchoWorks - SRE), Priya Rao (EchoWorks - Eng Mgmt)

Summary: quick technical deep dive to debug prefix reuse failures and repeated evictions on long-context LLM workloads. Showed internal prefetch/paging behaviors on Redwood runtime, discussed NVMe spill patterns, batching tradeoffs, quantized model artifacts, and on-prem/VPC concerns. Agreed next steps: exchange logs, run bench, and iterate prefix heuristics.

Topics discussed: prefetching strategy, eviction thresholds, KV paging to NVMe, prefix reuse heuristics, long-context cache fragmentation, batching windows, quantization side-effects (4-bit vs 8-bit), and on-prem IO constraints / KMS considerations.

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate, auto-transcribed, some mis-hearings):
[00:00:05] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — Olivia from our infra team is gonna drive the deep dive.
[00:00:12] Olivia: hi all, thanks. Maya, can you give a 2-minute overview of the workload that's showing the issues?
[00:00:20] Maya: yeah sure, so we're running a multi-turn summarization + retrieval pipeline. Typical session is 15–20k tokens, with lots of short prompts in between, and we keep prefix context from past turns to try to maintain persona. We're seeing consistent evictions in the KV store around the 8k–12k mark and then a bunch of paging thrash.
[00:00:38] Aaron: to add, the infra we're using for the PoC is an mGPU setup with NVMe attached, and sometimes the NVMe queues spike during peak regen. We're not on-prem yet, but this mirrors what we expect when we move to the private deployment.
[00:00:50] Olivia: ok. quick check — are you using prefix reuse aggressively (i.e., reusing the same KV keys for repeated system prompts)?
[00:00:57] Maya: yes, we canonicalize the first 2k tokens as a system prefix and try to reuse that object, but we still see duplicate entries in the cache and thens it evicts older session frame — sorry thens -> then it evicts. transcriber: "thens" shows up.
[00:01:10] Samir: cool, we'll look at three axes: 1) eviction policy and thresholds, 2) paging/prefetch behavior to NVMe, 3) prefix reuse hash collisions or mis-keying.

[00:01:28] Olivia: background on our KV layer — it's sharded by model+session id. Each shard has a soft TTL and an LRU-ish eviction but we also have a proactive prefetcher: when we detect likely next-token windows we pre-warm adjacent KV pages into memory. That prefetcher has heuristics tuned for median seq lengths. For long-context it sometimes misfires and paged pages evict others.
[00:01:54] Priya: when you say pages, are those 512KB or 1MB blocks? in our infra the NVMe mapping is 1MB.
[00:02:01] Olivia: good question — on our runtime the page size is configurable; defaults are 512KB but for quantized small models we sometimes push 1MB to reduce indexing overhead. That choice changes eviction granularity.
[00:02:12] Aaron: ah that may explain the big eviction jumps. We set the default to 1MB in the PoC to minimize metadata ops.

[00:02:22] [00:02:25] Maya: can you explain the prefetch heuristic? we saw bursts of IO right before a session hits 9k tokens, and then everything craps out.
[00:02:33] Olivia: sure. Heuristic is: if a session has steady token rate for N recent requests and the next-request size is > X, we prefetch K neighbouring KV pages up to a cap. The bug we've seen in long-context: the heuristic mis-estimates because of repeated short edits mid-session, so prefetch chases a rapidly-growing working set and ends up pulling in pages that evict other active sessions.
[00:02:56] Samir: note — that pattern is more common when prefix reuse fails: the runtime treats slightly-different prompt hashes as new keys, causing multiple near-duplicate entries. Prefetch then pulls duplicates for the same logical prefix.

[00:03:10] Aaron: so could prefix hashing be unstable because of whitespace changes or JSON ordering differences in our prompt serialization?
[00:03:16] Olivia: yes — we convert prompts to canonicalized bytes but there's a small bug where trailing nulls from the embedding pipeline slip in. That can cause different hashes.
[00:03:26] Maya: omg that matches what we saw; our preprocessor was adding a trailing delimiter for multi-doc prompts.
[00:03:33] Samir: quick mitigation: we can add a normalization layer on the runtime side to trim known noise and apply stable hashing. We'll share a patch that does that as a config flag.

[00:03:45] [00:04:00] Priya: on the paging side, how do you decide which KV to evict when a page must be spilled? is it strictly LRU or do you have cost-weighted eviction?
[00:04:09] Olivia: current default is LRU with a small age-bias for smaller keys — but we also support a cost model where entries with high reuse frequency get a retention bonus. For your workload the eviction decisions were mostly LRU because the prefetch pulled new pages that looked "hot" but weren't actually reused.
[00:04:25] Priya: could we tune the bias to favor session-affine prefixes? so that a user's session stays resident longer?
[00:04:31] Olivia: yep — we have a session-affinity weight. The tradeoff is it raises p99 tail for other sessions if your workload is dominating memory. For enterprise customers we expose a per-tenant reservation and adjustable soft limits.

[00:04:45] [00:05:10] Maya: you mentioned quantization earlier — can quantization cause larger KV entries? we're seeing bigger KB footprints for 4-bit quantized attention states.
[00:05:18] Olivia: good point. Quantization changes per-token state size because quantized KV caches may include dequantization metadata or alignment padding. In some backends a 4-bit packing increases CPU-side buffers and alignment can round up to a larger block, so effective sizes can be slightly larger than naive estimates. That plus 1MB page size can amplify eviction churn.
[00:05:39] Samir: TL;DR: smaller page sizes + corrected hashing + tuned prefetch windows should reduce churn.

[00:05:52] [00:06:10] Aaron: what about batching? we've toyed with 64ms batching windows to improve throughput — but that inflates latency a bit. Does batching interact with prefetch / eviction?
[00:06:18] Olivia: yes. Larger batching windows increase the simultaneous working set on GPU and the KV read bursts. If prefetch runs concurrently with large batches you'll see bigger IO bursts and more eviction pressure. For low-latency workloads we recommend smaller batch windows (5–20ms) and per-model batch caps.
[00:06:36] Maya: interesting — our initial config had both batch windows and aggressive prefetch which likely compounded.

[00:06:45] [00:07:10] Priya: on private deployments — what changes? we plan to move to our VPC environment with local NVMe arrays. Are there extra tuning knobs for on-prem?
[00:07:20] Olivia: yes, for private you get control plane telemetry and we provide a tuned defaults file for on-prem disks. Key knobs: page size, prefetch cap, session-affinity weight, and async-writeback thresholds. Also, if you're on-prem with high-latency backing store we can enable a multi-tier cache: in-RAM first, then local NVMe, then remote object store.
[00:07:42] Aaron: KMS / encryption? if KV spills to NVMe we need disk encryption and KMS integration.
[00:07:48] Samir: we support KMS/HSM integrations and envelope encryption. For Private we can handshake with your KMS and ensure keys never leave HSM. We'll send the compliance note.

[00:07:58] [00:08:25] Olivia: want to demo a repro quickly? I have a small run that shows prefetch chasing and the eviction spike.
[00:08:32] Maya: yes please.
[00:08:35] Olivia: (screen-share) starting a synthetic session. This session simulates repeated short updates with a persistent 2k prefix. Watch the KV resident set and IO counters.
[00:08:50] [00:09:05] Olivia: initial steady state — resident pages ~ 420MB. At request 120 we see the prefetcher pull 3 pages (prefetch K=3) — you can see IO spike to 120MB/s and resident set jumps to 1.1GB, then eviction of older sessions occurs.
[00:09:23] Maya: that matches our telemetry — sudden 1GB jump then a bunch of sessions timed out.
[00:09:30] Aaron: how do you surface those events in logs? we saw a bunch of "page_evicted" events but lacked context for why prefetch ran.
[00:09:38] Olivia: logs include prefetch decisions, trigger heuristics, and causal session IDs in the latest runtime. Older versions were sparse. We'll correlate your logs with the new richer ones.

[00:09:50] [00:10:15] Samir: recap of the likely root causes for EchoWorks: 1) hashing instability due to preprocessor noise -> prefix duplication 2) page size = 1MB creating large eviction granularity 3) aggressive prefetch heuristic + larger batching window amplifying IO bursts 4) quantization alignment increasing per-entry sizes.

[00:10:32] Maya: sounds right. Which fixes are low-friction? we want to try something that doesn't require private deploy.
[00:10:39] Olivia: quick low-friction items: change runtime config to 512KB page size, flip on the prefix-normalization patch, reduce prefetch K to 1, and reduce batch window to 20ms. Those are runtime flags and can be toggled on hosted tier for your account. We'll provide a rollout plan.
[00:10:55] Priya: what's the expected improvement?
[00:10:58] Olivia: based on bench, p50 tokens/sec may drop slightly but p95/p99 tail should improve by ~30–60% — we'll validate.

[00:11:10] [00:11:30] Aaron: any caveats with quantized models? if we change page size will that affect alignment and potentially make sizes worse?
[00:11:38] Olivia: it's model-dependent. For some 4-bit kernels smaller pages reduce padding waste; for others they increase metadata overhead. We'll include model-specific suggestions in the config diff.

[00:11:50] Maya: ok, let's talk measurement — what artifacts do you need from us to reproduce?
[00:11:55] Olivia: ideally: 1) a sample of anonymized prompt/session traces (token-level), 2) KV eviction logs and prefetch events for a 48-hour window, 3) the exact model name + quantization config, 4) batch window and batching params.

[00:12:12] Maya: we'll share that. Aaron can collect the logs.
[00:12:16] Aaron: yeah I can pull logs. Do you need raw NVMe iostat traces too?
[00:12:19] Olivia: NVMe perf counters are helpful — queue depth, latencies. Also OS-level throttles. We'll take anything you can provide.

[00:12:28] [00:12:45] Samir: timeline proposal: Maya uploads logs by Monday (2025-08-18), we run bench and reproduce by Thursday (2025-08-21), and then we schedule a follow-up with an on-prem/PoC plan for the following week.

[00:12:55] Priya: sounds good. any immediate guardrails to prevent repeated evictions in prod before the fix?
[00:13:00] Olivia: yes — throttling prefetch (K=0), enabling session-affinity weight, and lowering page size are the fastest. We'll give the exact commands.

[00:13:10] [00:13:40] Maya: side question — we use SSO and strict audit logging. if we go private how does Redwood handle audit retention for per-token traces? storage costs are a concern.
[00:13:50] Samir: audit retention is configurable per-customer; we can stream logs to your S3 and rotate. For sensitive traces we can redact or hash content and keep token counts only. We'll include options in the compliance doc.

[00:14:05] Olivia: one more note on prefix reuse heuristics — we can implement a "soft-canonicalization" stage that tries exact-match then fuzzy-match within a small edit distance; that reduces duplicate keys from whitespace/noise. But fuzzy introduces CPU cost and potential false matches. We'll prototype it as an opt-in feature.
[00:14:24] Maya: fuzzy match sounds risky but interesting. would like to see metrics on false-positive rate.

[00:14:32] Samir: we'll run experiments and give FP/FN numbers.

[00:14:45] [00:15:00] (discussion drifts into config flags and exact CLI for toggles; Olivia reads command snippets and the team copies them)

[00:25:10] [mid-call deep technical exchange — timestamps skip in transcript for brevity but exist in logs]
[00:25:12] Olivia: show bench script (synthetic) where we vary prefetch K and page size and measure p50/p95/p99 and NVMe throughput. Here are some quick numbers: (1) K=3, page=1MB -> p99 latency 2.9s, NVMe 160MB/s; (2) K=1, page=512KB -> p99 1.8s, NVMe 82MB/s; (3) K=0, page=512KB, batch-window 20ms -> p99 1.5s, NVMe 40MB/s.
[00:25:40] Priya: nice. does that hold with quantized 4-bit bfloat kernels?
[00:25:45] Olivia: slightly different numbers — alignment increased effective page occupancy by ~8% on the 4-bit kernel in our lab. We'll include that model-quantization delta in the findings.

[00:26:10] Maya: if we go to private on-prem, can the prefetch be disabled fully? we might prefer deterministic eviction rather than speculative IO.
[00:26:18] Olivia: yes, prefetch can be fully disabled. In private mode we often ship customers with prefetch off by default for constrained IO disks.

[00:26:30] Aaron: are there instrumentation changes we should add server-side that will help triage in future?
[00:26:36] Olivia: recommended instrumentation: per-request KV-hit/miss flags, prefetch triggers with decision context, page-size annotated evict events, and per-session resident footprint. We also suggest a rolling window heatmap for session affinity.

[00:26:50] [00:27:05] Samir: I'll attach a sample LogQL and an example Grafana dashboard for these metrics.

[00:27:20] Maya: great. small question — does Redwood's smart-routing affect KV locality? we sometimes route a session across nodes for cost reasons.
[00:27:30] Olivia: yes, routing can move sessions across shards if the policy demands it. We have sticky routing by default for session affinity; only certain cost-saving fallbacks will re-home sessions. If sessions get re-homed frequently it will destroy locality and increase page misses.

[00:27:45] Aaron: we do have autoscale events firing that reassign capacity. is that a red flag?
[00:27:50] Olivia: autoscale that moves shards mid-session is a problem for KV locality; we can set a cooldown so active sessions are never moved while active.

[00:28:05] [00:28:20] Maya: ok let's recap and confirm next steps verbally.
[00:28:25] Samir: recap: (1) EchoWorks to provide anonymized logs + NVMe traces by 2025-08-18, (2) Redwood to run bench and share results by 2025-08-21, (3) Redwood to provide runtime config diff and prefix-normalization patch by 2025-08-20, (4) follow-up PoC on-prem sync to be scheduled week of 2025-08-25.
[00:28:45] Priya: agreed.
[00:28:48] Maya: one more ask — can you send a quick how-to for toggling prefetch K and page size in hosted console?
[00:28:54] Olivia: yes, I'll send exact steps and a one-liner curl for the flags.
